newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-CANBERRA WATCH-Labour market slipping away from forecasts.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-CANBERRA WATCH-Labour market slipping away from forecasts.

text.p: The labour market forecasts in the budget, just seven weeks old, might be in trouble already.
Simple back-of-the-envelope calculations show that the government needs a sharp rise in labour force growth rates to achieve the 1.5 percent year-average employment growth forecast on August 20.

In fact, the economy will have to average 16,000 new jobs a month for the rest of the year, compared with the September trend rise of just 11,000, which was itself something of an improvement on the falls recorded before the March election.
Similarly, the budget forecasts now demand a 3,000-a-month fall in the number of unemployed people for the rest of the year, compared with the trend rise of 4,500 in September.
Without that shift, the 1996/97 year-average unemployment rate will not be the forecast 8.5 percent.

And the longer it takes for the labour market to improve, the higher will be the run rate required. Since there is no evidence of an immediate turnaround, we can probably assume that the budget forecasts will not be met unless much bigger improvements emerge later this financial year.
That's the analysis of what is needed to meet the forecast.
More disturbing is what will happen if nothing changes.

If the latest trend movements in employment, unemployment and workforce growth were repeated in all the remaining months of the fiscal year, then the unemployment rate by June 1997 will be 9.0 percent, with a June quarter average of 8.9 percent -- nowhere near the forecast 8.25 percent.
On similar assumptions, the year-average unemployment rate would be 8.8 percent, while employment growth would be just 1.25 percent.
Finally, all of this has implications for the budget, which -- as Wednesday's Canberra Watch observed -- shows no signs yet of the rapid improvement needed to meet its targets.
A 0.25 percent shortfall in employment numbers implies a loss of about A$150 million in pay-as-you-earn tax receipts.
More seriously, a 0.4-percentage-point blowout in the unemployment rate suggests an extra A$350 million on the social security bill.
